<!-- theorema-1: body_md -->
Let $T$ be a $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module and put $C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$. Assume that
$$
d=\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})<\infty.
$$
If
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(T,T)=0\quad(1\leq i\leq d+2),
$$
then $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
<!-- end theorema-1 -->
<!-- theoremb-1: body_md -->
If a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module $T$ is not a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module, then
$$
\operatorname{findim}\nolimits\bigl((A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T))^{\rm op}\bigr)=\infty.
$$
In fact, $A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$ has finitely generated left modules of every prescribed positive finite projective dimension.
<!-- end theoremb-1 -->
<!-- theoremc-1: body_md -->
Let $A$ be an Artin algebra with $\operatorname{rad}\nolimits^3 A=0$. Then every self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
<!-- end theoremc-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:tilting}
A right $A$-module $T\in\mathsf{mod}\hspace{.01in}A$ is called a \emph{classical $1$-tilting module} if the following conditions hold.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item $\operatorname{pd}\nolimits_A T\leq1$.
\item $\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^1(T,T)=0$.
\item $|T|=|A|$.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:tau-tilting}
Let $T\in\mathsf{mod}\hspace{.01in}A$. The right $A$-module $T$ is called $\tau$-rigid if
$$
\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(T,\tau T)=0.
$$
It is called $\tau$-tilting if it is $\tau$-rigid and $|T|=|A|$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:selforthogonal}
A right $A$-module $T\in\mathsf{mod}\hspace{.01in}A$ is called \emph{self-orthogonal} if
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(T,T)=0\quad(i\geq1).
$$
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:quotient-tilting}
Let $T$ be a $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module. Put
$$
I=\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T),\quad C=A/I.
$$
Then $I\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A$, and $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $C$-module. Moreover, $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module if and only if $I=0$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By \cite[Proposition~2.2(a)]{AIR}, every $\tau$-tilting module is sincere. More precisely, \cite[Proposition~2.5(3)]{CLZZ} shows that the annihilator of a $\tau$-tilting module is nilpotent. Hence $I\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A$. By \cite[Proposition~2.2(c)]{AIR}, the right $C$-module $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting module. Since $T$ is $\tau$-tilting, \cite[Proposition~2.2(b)]{AIR} implies that $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module exactly when it is faithful. Thus this happens exactly when $I=0$. The quotient viewpoint is also developed in \cite[Theorem~3.5]{CLZZ}.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:findim}
Let $\Gamma$ be an Artin algebra. Its \emph{little finitistic dimension} is
$$
\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(\Gamma)=\sup\{\operatorname{pd}\nolimits_\Gamma X\mid X\in\mathsf{mod}\,\Gamma,\ \operatorname{pd}\nolimits_\Gamma X<\infty\}.
$$
Thus $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})$ is computed on finitely generated left $C$-modules.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:radical-epi}
Let $\Gamma$ be an Artin algebra. Let $f:P\to Q$ be a radical morphism between finitely generated projective right $\Gamma$-modules. If $Q\neq0$, then $f$ is not an epimorphism.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Suppose that $f$ is an epimorphism. Since $Q$ is projective, there is a morphism $s:Q\to P$ such that $fs=1_Q$. The radical is an ideal, so $fs$ belongs to $\operatorname{rad}\nolimits\operatorname{End}\nolimits_\Gamma(Q)$. This is impossible for a nonzero module $Q$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:dual-radical}
Let $I\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A$ and put $C=A/I$. Let $u:P'\to P$ be a radical morphism between finitely generated projective right $A$-modules. Then $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(P,C)$ and $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(P',C)$ are finitely generated projective left $C$-modules. The induced map
$$
\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(u,C):\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(P,C)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(P',C)
$$
is radical. Moreover, its image is contained in the radical of $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(P',C)$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The first statement follows because $P$ and $P'$ are direct summands of finite direct sums of copies of $A$. We have $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(A,C)\cong C$ as left $C$-modules.

For the second statement, decompose $P$ and $P'$ into indecomposable projective summands. It is enough to consider a component
$$
v:eA\longrightarrow fA,
$$
where $e$ and $f$ are primitive idempotents. Under the standard identification
$$
\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(eA,fA)\cong fAe,
$$
a radical morphism corresponds to an element of $f(\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A)e$. Applying $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(-,C)$ gives a map
$$
Cf\longrightarrow Ce
$$
whose defining element is the image of that element in $fCe$. Since
$$
\operatorname{rad}\nolimits C=(\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A)/I,
$$
this image belongs to $f(\operatorname{rad}\nolimits C)e$. Hence each component of $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(u,C)$ is radical. Therefore $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(u,C)$ is a radical morphism between finitely generated projective left $C$-modules. The same component calculation gives
$\operatorname{Im}\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(u,C)\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\nolimits\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(P',C).$
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:vanishing-transfer}
Let $m\geq2$. Assume that
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(T,T)=0\quad(1\leq i\leq m).
$$
Then
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^j(C,C)=0\quad(1\leq j\leq m-1).
$$
In particular, if $T$ is self-orthogonal, then
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^j(C,C)=0\qquad(j\geq1).
$$
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Apply $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(-,T)$ to \eqref{eq:tilting-C}. Since $T_0,T_1\in\mathsf{add}\hspace{.01in} T$, the long exact sequence gives
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^j(C,T)=0\qquad(1\leq j\leq m-1).
$$
The same vanishing holds when $T$ is replaced by $T_0$ or $T_1$.

Now apply $\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(C,-)$ to \eqref{eq:tilting-C}. For every $C$-module $M$, evaluation at $1+I$ gives a natural isomorphism
$$
\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(C,M)\cong M.
$$
Under these isomorphisms, the map
$$
\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(C,T_0)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(C,T_1)
$$
is the epimorphism $T_0\to T_1$ in \eqref{eq:tilting-C}. It follows that $\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^1(C,C)=0$.

For $2\leq j\leq m-1$, the long exact sequence contains
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^{j-1}(C,T_1)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^j(C,C)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^j(C,T_0).
$$
The two outer terms vanish. Hence $\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^j(C,C)=0$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:finite-range}
The finite range in Proposition~\ref{prop:vanishing-transfer} is essential for the quantitative form of the main theorem. Full self-orthogonality is not needed once a bound for $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})$ is available. This distinguishes the result from the finite projective dimension criterion in \cite[Theorem~3.4]{Zhang}, where the hypothesis concerns $\operatorname{pd}\nolimits_A T$ itself.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
Let $T$ be a $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module. Put
$$
I=\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T),\quad C=A/I.
$$
Assume that
$$
d=\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})<\infty.
$$
If
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(T,T)=0\quad(1\leq i\leq d+2),
$$
then $I=0$. Hence $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Suppose that $I\neq0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:vanishing-transfer},
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(C,C)=0\quad(1\leq i\leq d+1).
$$
Thus \eqref{eq:dual-complex} is exact at $Q_i$ for $1\leq i\leq d+1$.

We claim that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Qi-nonzero}
Q_i\neq0\quad(1\leq i\leq d+2).
\end{equation}
Since $I\neq0$, the projective module $P_1$ is nonzero. Let $eA$ be a nonzero indecomposable projective summand of $P_1$. The idempotent $e$ does not belong to $I$ because $I\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A$. Hence
$$
\operatorname{Hom}\nolimits_A(eA,C)\cong Ce\neq0.
$$
It follows that $Q_1\neq0$.

Assume that $Q_r\neq0$ for some $1\leq r\leq d+1$. If $Q_{r+1}=0$, exactness at $Q_r$ implies that the preceding map onto $Q_r$ is an epimorphism. For $r=1$, the preceding map is $\delta_0=0$, which is impossible. For $r\geq2$, the preceding map is radical. We apply Lemma~\ref{lem:radical-epi} to $C^{\rm op}$ and obtain a contradiction. This proves \eqref{eq:Qi-nonzero}.

Set
$$
X=\operatorname{Coker}(\delta_{d+1}:Q_{d+1}\to Q_{d+2}).
$$
By \eqref{eq:Qi-nonzero}, $Q_{d+2}\neq0$. The map $\delta_{d+1}$ is radical. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:radical-epi} to $C^{\rm op}$ shows that it is not an epimorphism. Hence $X\neq0$. Exactness gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:X-resolution}
0\longrightarrow Q_1\longrightarrow Q_2\longrightarrow\cdots
\longrightarrow Q_{d+1}\longrightarrow Q_{d+2}\longrightarrow X\longrightarrow0.
\end{equation}
Every differential between the projective terms is radical. The kernel of $Q_{d+2}\to X$ is contained in $\operatorname{rad}\nolimits Q_{d+2}$. Hence this epimorphism is a projective cover. Therefore \eqref{eq:X-resolution} is the minimal projective resolution of $X$. Since $Q_1\neq0$, we obtain
$$
\operatorname{pd}\nolimits_{{}_C}X=d+1.
$$
Here $X$ is a finitely generated left $C$-module. Equivalently, it is a finitely generated right $C^{\rm op}$-module. This contradicts $d=\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})$.

Therefore $I=0$. The conclusion now follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-tilting}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:selforthogonal}
Let $T$ be a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module and put $C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$. If
$$
\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})<\infty,
$$
then $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
This follows immediately from Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:counterexample}
Let $T$ be a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module which is not a classical $1$-tilting module. Put
$$
C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T).
$$
Then
$$
\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})=\infty.
$$
For every $n\geq1$, there is a finitely generated left $C$-module $X_n$ with
$$
\operatorname{pd}\nolimits_{{}_C}X_n=n.
$$
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Since $T$ is self-orthogonal, Proposition~\ref{prop:vanishing-transfer} gives $\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(C,C)=0$ for all $i\geq1$. Since $T$ is not tilting, Proposition~\ref{prop:quotient-tilting} gives $I=\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)\neq0$. Thus the argument in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} works in every degree.

For $n\geq1$, set
$$
X_n=\operatorname{Coker}(Q_n\longrightarrow Q_{n+1}).
$$
The exact sequence
$$
0\longrightarrow Q_1\longrightarrow Q_2\longrightarrow\cdots
\longrightarrow Q_{n+1}\longrightarrow X_n\longrightarrow0
$$
is a minimal projective resolution. Hence $\operatorname{pd}\nolimits_{{}_C}X_n=n$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:FDC}
If the little finitistic dimension conjecture holds for all Artin algebras, then every self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module, that is, the self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting conjecture holds for all Artin algebras.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
For a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module $T$, the quotient $C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$ is again an Artin algebra. The finitistic dimension conjecture gives $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})<\infty$. Corollary~\ref{cor:selforthogonal} applies.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:comparison}
Corollaries~\ref{cor:selforthogonal} and \ref{cor:counterexample} give two complementary readings of the same argument. On the positive side, finite little finitistic dimension of the annihilator quotient forces a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting module to be faithful. On the negative side, a genuine counterexample forces the opposite quotient to have infinite little finitistic dimension. More is true in the negative direction because the proof constructs modules of every positive finite projective dimension.

This obstruction is different from the one in \cite{ZhangII}, which involves the endomorphism algebra $\operatorname{End}\nolimits_A(T)^{\rm op}$. It is also different from the delooping criterion in \cite[Theorem~5.4]{CLZZ}. Our criterion is formulated entirely in terms of $A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$. None of these conditions is claimed to imply the others in general.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:radical-cube-zero}
Let $T$ be a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module and put
$$
C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T).
$$
If
$$
\operatorname{rad}\nolimits^3 C=0,
$$
then $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The opposite algebra also satisfies $\operatorname{rad}\nolimits^3(C^{\rm op})=0$. By Green and Zimmermann-Huisgen \cite{GreenHuisgen},
$$
\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})<\infty.
$$
The conclusion follows from Corollary~\ref{cor:selforthogonal}.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:radical-cube-zero}
Let $A$ be an Artin algebra with $\operatorname{rad}\nolimits^3 A=0$. Then every self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module, that is, the self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting conjecture holds.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
Let $I=\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$ and $C=A/I$. Since $I\subseteq\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A$, we have
$$
\operatorname{rad}\nolimits C=(\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A)/I.
$$
Hence $\operatorname{rad}\nolimits^3 C=0$. The result follows from Theorem~\ref{thm:radical-cube-zero}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{rem:radical-square}
Zhang \cite{ZhangII} proved the radical square zero case by annihilator separation. Theorem~\ref{thm:radical-cube-zero} extends that positive result to radical cube zero algebras. The proof is quite different. It uses the minimal $A$-projective resolution of the annihilator quotient and the theorem of Green and Zimmermann-Huisgen \cite{GreenHuisgen}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:cube-rep-infinite}
Let $k$ be an infinite field. Let $Q$ be the quiver with two vertices, one arrow $\alpha:1\to2$, and two loops $x,y$ at vertex $2$. Let $J$ be the arrow ideal of $kQ$. Put
$$
A=kQ/(J^3,xy-yx).
$$
Then $A$ is connected and nonlocal. Moreover,
$$
(\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A)^3=0
\quad\text{and}\quad
(\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A)^2\neq0.
$$
Hence Corollary~\ref{cor:radical-cube-zero} shows that every self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.

(1) We first show that $A$ is representation-infinite.

Let $e_1$ be the idempotent at the first vertex. Then
$$
R=A/Ae_1A\cong k[x,y]/(x,y)^3.
$$
The quotient $R/(x,y)^2$ is $k[x,y]/(x,y)^2$. For each $\lambda\in k$, let $M_\lambda$ be the two-dimensional right $R/(x,y)^2$-module with basis $u_\lambda,v_\lambda$ and action
$$
u_\lambda x=v_\lambda,\quad
u_\lambda y=\lambda v_\lambda,\quad
v_\lambda x=v_\lambda y=0.
$$
Each $M_\lambda$ has simple top, and hence it is indecomposable. A direct comparison of the actions of $x$ and $y$ gives
$$
M_\lambda\simeq M_\mu
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\lambda=\mu.
$$
Thus $R$, and hence $A$, is representation-infinite. Since $R$ is a proper representation-infinite quotient of $A$, the algebra $A$ is not minimal representation-infinite.

(2) We next show that $A$ is not Iwanaga--Gorenstein.

The socle of the commutative local algebra $R$ is
$$
\operatorname{soc}R=(x,y)^2,
$$
which has dimension $3$ over $k$. By Bruns and Herzog \cite[Theorem~3.2.10]{BrunsHerzog}, a zero-dimensional commutative local ring is Gorenstein if and only if it has type one. Equivalently, its socle is one-dimensional over the residue field. Thus $R$ is not Gorenstein. Hence
$$
\operatorname{id}_R R=\infty.
$$
As a right $A$-module, $e_2A$ is naturally identified with $R$. Hence every finitely generated projective right $R$-module is projective as a right $A$-module. A projective $R$-resolution of a right $R$-module $X$, viewed by restriction of scalars along $A\to R$, is therefore also an $A$-projective resolution. It follows that
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^n(X,e_2A)\cong\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_R^n(X,R)
$$
for every finitely generated right $R$-module $X$ and every $n\geq0$. Since $A_A=e_1A\oplus e_2A$, we obtain
$$
\operatorname{id}_A A=\infty.
$$
Thus $A$ is not Iwanaga--Gorenstein.

In particular, this example is outside the local, syzygy-finite Gorenstein, representation-finite, minimal representation-infinite, and radical square zero cases recalled in the introduction.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:representation-finite}
Let $T$ be a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module and put $C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$. If $C$ is representation-finite, then $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
The standard duality for Artin algebras identifies finite representation type on the right and on the left \cite{ARS}. Hence there are only finitely many isomorphism classes of indecomposable finitely generated left $C$-modules. Their finite projective dimensions are bounded. Thus $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})<\infty$, and Corollary~\ref{cor:selforthogonal} applies.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{rem:repfinite}
When $A$ itself is representation-finite, Corollary~\ref{cor:representation-finite} recovers the known positive answer from \cite[Proposition~5.3]{CLZZ}. The quotient formulation is slightly more flexible. It only asks that the particular algebra $A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$ attached to $T$ be representation-finite.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:finite-test}
Let $T$ be a $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module and put $C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$. Assume that
$$
\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})\leq d.
$$
If
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(T,T)=0\quad(1\leq i\leq d+2),
$$
then $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:main} with $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})\leq d$. If the actual finitistic dimension is smaller than $d$, the assumed vanishing contains the range needed in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:finite-range-test}
Let $T$ be a $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module and put $C=A/\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)$.
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item If $C$ is hereditary and
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^i(T,T)=0\quad(1\leq i\leq3),
$$
then $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
\item If $C$ is semisimple and
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^1(T,T)=0=\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^2(T,T),
$$
then $T$ is a classical $1$-tilting right $A$-module.
\end{enumerate}
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
If $C$ is hereditary, then $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})\leq1$. If $C$ is semisimple, then $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})=0$. Both assertions follow from Proposition~\ref{prop:finite-test}.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
\label{ex:excluded-annihilator}
Let $A$ be the algebra in Example~\ref{ex:cube-rep-infinite} and put
$$
I=\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A.
$$
Since $A$ has two simple modules,
$$
C=A/I\cong k\times k
$$
is semisimple. Hence $\operatorname{findim}\nolimits(C^{\rm op})=0$.

Suppose that a $\tau$-tilting right $A$-module $T$ satisfies
$$
\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)=I
$$
and
$$
\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^1(T,T)=0=\operatorname{Ext}\nolimits_A^2(T,T).
$$
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} with $d=0$ gives $\operatorname{Ann}\nolimits_A(T)=0$, contrary to $I\neq0$. Therefore no such $T$ exists. This illustrates the finite form of our criterion. On this algebra, the first two self-extension groups already exclude $\operatorname{rad}\nolimits A$ as the annihilator of a $\tau$-tilting module.
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{rem:final}
The main theorem narrows the search for a counterexample. A nonzero annihilator alone is not enough. The corresponding quotient must have infinite little finitistic dimension. In fact, it must contain finitely generated left modules of every positive finite projective dimension. This is only a necessary condition. The existence of such a quotient does not imply the existence of a self-orthogonal $\tau$-tilting module with nonzero annihilator.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
